opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so at the time, the dominant view in the field was that behavior cloning was the naive baseline. You learn a mapping from observations to actions from demonstrations, and everyone "knew" it suffered from compounding errors and distribution shift: you drift a little off the expert's trajectory, you end up in states you've never seen, and things fall apart. So the excitement was mostly around reinforcement learning, with the agent discovering behavior through trial and error.

What struck me about the DeepMind results was that, with enough data and the right model, imitation got you surprisingly far, often much further than people expected from something supposedly so simple. That made me step back and ask whether the problem was ever behavior cloning itself, or the scale, data quality, and representations we were feeding it.

For robotics specifically, that question matters a lot. RL on real robots is painfully expensive. You can't run millions of episodes on a physical arm, the robot breaks, someone has to reset the scene, and designing reward functions for everyday manipulation tasks is a research problem of its own. Demonstrations, by contrast, are something humans can actually give. A person can teleoperate a robot and show it how to set a table in a few minutes. So if imitation scales the way those results suggested, it's a far more practical path to robots that do useful things.

The other piece was that behavior cloning turns robot learning into something that looks more like supervised learning, which is where deep learning has been most reliable. You get stable training and you can lean on all the progress in vision and sequence modeling. The compounding error problem doesn't vanish, but you can attack it with better data collection, better policy architectures, and structure like hierarchy or task decomposition, rather than abandoning the approach.

So my takeaway was that this "simple baseline" was underrated, and the interesting research questions were: how do we collect the right data, how do we make these policies generalize, and how do we scale them up? That's shaped a lot of what I've worked on since.

r001.rationale: The response discusses imitation from demonstrations and its promise, but does not say the demonstrations were filtered to remove suboptimal behavior or that this enabled strong task performance without reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It notes that people can teleoperate robots to provide demonstrations, but does not identify insufficient development of effective teleoperation methods as a gap in academic robotics research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that for a long time behavior cloning was kind of the thing everyone dismissed. You learn it in a class, you see the compounding error argument from DAgger, and you file it away as a baseline that doesn't really work. I was in that camp too.

What changed for me was seeing what DeepMind was doing with large-scale imitation, like the robot manipulation work and later things like RT-1 and Gato-style setups. The results weren't magical in terms of the algorithm. It was still supervised learning on demonstrations. But the scale and the diversity of the data, plus a reasonably expressive model, pushed performance far past what I would have predicted from the theory. The failure mode we all worried about, that small errors drift you off the data manifold and everything collapses, just showed up a lot less when the data covered enough of the space.

That made me rethink where the bottleneck actually is. A lot of us had been putting effort into clever learning objectives, reinforcement learning, reward design, and so on, because we assumed the algorithm was the hard part. But those results suggested that if you have a simple objective that scales cleanly with data, the data and the model architecture may matter more than the learning signal. Behavior cloning is about the simplest objective you can have. It's stable, it's easy to debug, and it's easy to scale on a cluster. You don't have the sample complexity and the instability that make RL on real robots painful.

And there's a second piece, which is that humans are actually pretty good at generating demonstrations, especially with better teleoperation interfaces. So the question became less about "how do we squeeze more out of a few demos" and more about "how do we build the pipeline where more demos keep translating into better policies." That's a very different research agenda, and to me it looked a lot more promising than where we'd been.

So I wouldn't say BC is solved or that the compounding error problem disappeared. It's still there, and you see it in long-horizon tasks. But I thought the community was under-investing in it relative to its potential, and that the right move was to take it seriously as a scaling problem rather than treating it as a toy baseline.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was that a relatively simple idea—learning to imitate demonstrations—could produce compelling robot behavior when you gave it enough good data. In robotics, we often focused on more elaborate methods because behavior cloning seemed too limited: the robot makes a small mistake, ends up somewhere unfamiliar, and doesn’t know how to recover.

Seeing DeepMind’s results made me think we should take that baseline much more seriously. How much of the limitation was the method itself, and how much was the scale and diversity of the demonstrations? That shifts the research question toward how we collect data and how well the resulting behavior generalizes. It doesn’t mean imitation solves everything, but it seemed like a foundation worth investing in.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation can produce compelling behavior with good data, but does not state that demonstrations are filtered to remove suboptimal behavior or that strong performance is achieved without reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was that behavior cloning was so simple, but it was actually working. In robotics, we had spent a lot of effort on reinforcement learning and more complicated approaches, while learning directly from demonstrations was often treated as a baseline. Seeing DeepMind’s results made me wonder whether we had dismissed it too quickly. Maybe the limitation wasn’t the basic idea; maybe we needed better data, more diverse demonstrations, and models that could use them effectively. That seemed worth taking seriously.
